\title{Checking a forecast put to Parliament: unbundling Canadian television, 2016--2019}
\author{Brett Reynolds \orcidlink{0000-0003-0073-7195}%

\begin{document}
\maketitle

\begin{abstract}
In 2016 MPs heard that new rules from Canada's broadcasting regulator (CRTC) would cost \lttvJobsTotal{} media jobs by 2020. I compare the intermediate predictions of the commissioned study behind that figure with CRTC data for 2016--2019, under a plan fixed before collecting outcomes; total jobs and causal effects aren't tested. At the designated error scales, specialty and pay channels' revenue, on which most of the job figure depends, lost less ground against the study's baseline than any cited uptake estimate implies, and distributors' revenue was consistent with the forecast. The study assumed \lttvByopSixteen{} of subscribers would take an entry-level package with chosen channels in 2016; the CRTC's mid-2016 entry-level share was \lttvUptakeJuneShare{}, and a 2017 survey outside the plan's sources put starter-package adoption near the study's \lttvByopSeventeen{} for 2017. In later analyses, per-subscriber affiliation payments to Canadian channels grew \lttvPerSubGrowth{} in 2015--2019, against the baseline carriage fee's \lttvBaseFeeGrowth{}, and, at those scales, only a low uptake path among those tested keeps both revenue series compatible with the study's partially recalculated chain. The testimony called an economy-wide estimate media jobs, described the study's 18\%, which its totals put at \lttvCPEShareTwenty{}, as a share of current spending, and omitted the uptake assumption.
\end{abstract}

\noindent\textbf{Keywords:} forecast evaluation; ex post analysis; economic impact studies; broadcasting regulation; Canada
